title: Exploring Earth and Environmental Sciences
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC1000.
description: (UGEB1870 is double-coded with EESC1001.) The course provides an interdisciplinary study of the Earth Systems, including natural phenomena in the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, cryosphere, and biosphere. The mechanism of these systems, associated dynamics and anthropogenic impacts will be introduced and discussed. The course also serves as a platform to understand and critically assess global environmental change, natural hazards, biodiversity loss, and the water-energy-food nexus, and explore potential technological and policy solutions to these problems. These objectives align strongly with the understanding and pursuit of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, especially SDG#7 Affordable and Clean Energy, SDG#13 Climate Action, SDG#14 Life Below Water, and SDG#15 Life on Land. In addition to attending lectures, students will visit the Jockey Club Museum of Climate Change where it displays the way scientists examine past and current climate and the factors leading to current global temperature change. A geological field excursion will be another highlight of the course to demonstrate the scientific concepts applied to reveal Earth’s tectonic history, evolution and interaction among various spheres. With diverse scientific topics in Earth’s systems, the course shows students how each Earth’s system is interlocking with other spheres and, hence raise the awareness in the importance of sustainability.
outcome: Describe and explain how the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, cryosphere, and biosphere interact and how feedback mechanisms operate among the Earth systems.  Develop an interdisciplinary approach for investigating Earth system dynamics.   Discuss the anthropogenic influences, as well as scientific and technical challenges related to global environmental changes, natural hazards, and the food-water-energy nexus critically.  Recognize the complexity of linkages between environmental pressures and human responses related to contemporary sustainable development challenges, contributing to the understanding and pursuit of SDG#7 Affordable and Clean Energy, SDG#13 Climate Action, SDG#14 Life below Water, and SDG#15 Life on Land.  Communicate effectively about Earth system and environmental issues in an appropriate science format (i.e. scientific poster and QnA) through working independently and collaboratively.
syllabus: Lectures: To provide students basic concepts of different spheres, background information about present environmental phenomena and scientific approaches to study the Earth system  Tutorial: To guide students critically think about Earth system and related issues to our environment.  Visit: To show students how professional field works to understand our Earth  Field trip: To facilitate students observe the environment and interpret and discuss related environmental problems   Note: Students are expected to attend all lectures, and participate in all tutorials, the visit and the field trip. Meeting with academic advisors can be arranged upon request.     Course Syllabus (English) (Tentative)  The course content will be divided into three parts:     Part I: Geosphere and Cryosphere (Week 1-5)  This component focuses on studying the solid Earth using gravity, electromagnetic and seismic methods. Students will be introduced to the solid physical foundations of the solid Earth, as well as an overview of the structure and composition of the Earth, its materials and constituents, dynamics of its internal and external processes.     Part II: Atmosphere and Climate (Week 7-9)  This compenent covers an integrated introduction to the climate system and the dynamics and chemistry of the atmosphere. Students will learn to explain the history, current state and future projection of weather and climate, natural hazards, and global climate change in the context of natural variability and anthropogenic influence.     Part III: Ecosystem Interactions (Week 10-12)  This compenent covers the interactions of the terrestrial and marine biosphere with the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere. title: Introductory Practical Course in Earth and Environmental Sciences
description: The Introductory Practical Course in Earth and Environmental Sciences is a project-based learning experience designed to introduce freshmen to Earth and Environmental Sciences through direct field observation and hands-on project work. This course will be led by 3 instructors in Geology and Geophysics, Atmospheric Sciences and Environmental Sciences. By exploring the geology beneath our feet, the atmospheric currents above us, and the environmental issues that surround us, students will gain a holistic understanding of our planet.

title: Environmental Monitoring with Mobile Technology
description: The Environmental Monitoring course is a project-based learning experience focusing on monitoring air and water quality using small handheld computers such as Raspberry Pi. Students will explore the fundamentals of sensor technology, data acquisition, and environmental analysis. Through hands-on projects, students will learn to design, build, and program portable monitoring devices capable of measuring air pollutants, water quality indicators, and environmental parameters. The course emphasizes real-world applications of environmental monitoring, encouraging students to critically assess and address local and global environmental challenges with innovative solutions.This course will be led by instructors specializing in environmental science, computer science, and engineering, providing a multidisciplinary approach to environmental monitoring.

title: Fundamental Earth and Environmental Field Study I
requirements: Not for students who have taken EESC2110 or ESSC2110.
description: EESC2009 is a fundamental field-based course introducing elementary concepts of past Earth’s processes and environmental changes. It also covers important aspects of plate tectonics, different rock types, geological deformation, geomorphology and environmental changes, natural hazards and human impacts. The principal goal of this course is to let students understand how the present geological records and landforms reveal the past tectonic movements and affect the human urban planning. Students are trained to observe, describe and discuss field features, with the help of field tools (e.g. compasses-clinometer and GPS receiver). Basic skills of field techniques, interpreting geologic maps and making field notes are introduced to assist students acquiring field data and discuss possible geologic processes. A field report from each group is required to summarize the field study logically. Field locations of this course may change from year to year. All students are welcome, but priority will be given to students who have taken EESC1001.

title: Solid Earth Dynamics
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC2010.
description: This course presents an integrated introduction to the solid earth system stressing the geological, chemical, physical, and biological interactions among the lithosphere, hydrosphere and cryosphere. The course applies basic scientific and mathematical concepts to explain the history and behaviour of the solid earth system. Geophysical and geochemical techniques for probing the interior of the earth are reviewed. Plate tectonics is introduced as a unifying theme to understand geodynamic processes. The course includes discussions of topics that are relevant to society, resources and sustainability, such as the physical and chemical basis of natural hazards (earthquakes, tsunami, landslides) and their mitigation, and the impact of geological processes on the global environment.
outcome: This course will contribute to the understanding of the dynamics of the solid Earth system, specifically the lithosphere, hydrosphere and cryosphere, as well as their interaction. The students should be able to: 1) describe and use the scientific process, explain how theories are built upon earth system observations, and how both are tested and revised; 2) explain how fundamental physical, chemical, and biological principles govern specific earth system processes; 3) participate knowledgeably and intelligently in discussions of public policy related to earth system science, particularly with respect to natural hazards, resources, environment and sustainable development; 4) work effectively in a team, and present information in a clear, concise and logical manner.

title: Climate System Dynamics
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC2020.
description: This course presents an integrated introduction to the climate system, stressing the dynamics of the atmosphere and its physical and chemical interactions with the hydrosphere, biosphere and geosphere. The course applies basic scientific and mathematical principles to explain the history, current state and future projection of weather and climate, natural hazards (e.g., typhoons, floods), and global climate change in the context of natural variability and anthropogenic influence. Topics include Earth’s energy balance, climate feedback, convection and clouds, general circulation of the atmosphere and ocean, biogeochemistry and global carbon cycle, roles of vegetation and ecosystems, and historical and future climate change. Student taking this course are expected to have taken PHYS1111, CHEM1070 and MATH1010 or equivalent.
outcome: This course will contribute to the understanding of the dynamics of the climate system, specifically the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and solid earth, as well as their interactions. title: Intermediate Geosciences Field Study II
requirements: Pre-requisite: (EESC2010 or ESSC2010) and with instructor's approval.
description: EESC2129 is designed to provide students with fundamental geological field techniques and the application of geological and environmental concepts specific to the region of Hong Kong. The course aims to deepen students' understanding of the local geology, including its formation processes, tectonic history, and its relationship with the environment. By the end of the course, students will have acquired a solid background in local geology and geomorphology. The course emphasizes hands-on training and practical skills development. Students will learn essential geological field techniques, including map reading, gathering geological data, making field observations, and jotting geological field notes. They will also develop critical thinking skills through the analysis and interpretation of geological data. Additionally, the course includes training in life-saving skills to ensure students' safety during fieldwork. EESC2129 consists of a 10-day local field study and five pre-trip lectures. The field study provides an immersive experience where students will directly apply the knowledge and techniques learned in the classroom to real geological settings in Hong Kong. The pre-trip lectures serve as a preparatory phase, covering relevant theoretical concepts, field methodologies, and safety protocols. Following the field study, two post-trip discussions will provide an opportunity for students to share their findings, and engage in further analysis and interpretation. Successful completion of EESC2129 requires continuous teamwork and independent assignments. Students will be expected to collaborate with their peers during fieldwork, share responsibilities, and contribute to group discussions. Additionally, independent assignments will be assigned to reinforce students' understanding of the course material and encourage individual exploration of specific geological topics.Note: This course may involve physical activities and fieldwork in outdoor environments. Students are advised to comply with safety guidelines, follow instructions from instructors, and maintain appropriate fitness levels to ensure a safe and enriching learning experience.

title: Minerals and Natural Resources
description: EESC2160 is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of minerals as fundamental building blocks of the Earth, their chemistry, occurrence, physical and chemical features, crystallography, as well as the formation and uses of naturally formed minerals, oil, and gas. The course also covers mining processes and management, exploring the interaction between natural resources and the environment, and their impact on the biological system. The course teaches students chemistry in the Solid Earth, occurrence, exploration and usage of natural resources like minerals, gas and oil. The course trains students with skills of identifying physical properties and chemical properties of natural forming minerals. Teachers will introduce techniques and technology in mining and extracting natural resources. Areas of interaction between natural resources and the environment, as well as the management of natural resources, will be elaborated in student’s problem-based learning sessions. Students are expected to equip knowledge and skills in understanding the real-world scenarios of the natural resources, and problem-solving skills in resource management practices and decision-making processes. These objectives align strongly with the understanding and pursuit of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, especially SDG#7 Affordable and Clean Energy, SDG#11 Raise the public awareness in urgent actions to combat climate change, and SDG#12 Promote responsibility in global environmental changes.
outcome: Upon completing this course, students will be able to: Describe the rock-forming minerals in terms of their chemistry, structural characteristics, and physical properties. Discuss the relationship between the chemical composition, structural features, and physical properties of minerals. Describe the mineral assemblages commonly found in igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. Understand the formation processes and practical applications of natural resources, including minerals, oil, and gas. Gain knowledge of mining processes and management techniques, including environmental considerations. Analyze the interaction between natural resources and the environment, as well as their impact on biological systems. Develop problem-solving skills through the application of natural resource management principles. Recognize the complexity and linkages among the natural resource exploration, associated impacts and environmental management.  Evaluate the needs of the present-day society and sustainable development challenges, contributing to the understanding and pursuit SDG#7 Affordable and Clean Energy, SDG#11 Raise the public awareness in urgent actions to combat climate change, and SDG#12 Promote responsibility in global environmental changes.

title: Environmental Chemistry
requirements: Not for students who have taken ENSC2515. Pre-requisite: EESC2270 or ENSC2270 or permission of the instructor.
description: This is a foundation course designed to equip students with a proper understanding of the fundamental aspects of environmental chemistry. It introduces the basic concept of chemical equilibrium and kinetics, the nature and characteristics of various common types of air and water pollution arising from industrial, agricultural and domestic sources. It outlines the principles of measurement for various parameters commonly used for air and water pollution studies, their significance and limitations. It also examines various types of aerial emission arising from combustion and industrial processes, and vehicles, and their chemical interaction leading to various global environmental issues such as the formation of photochemical smog, depletion of ozone layer and global warming effects.

title: Structural Geology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC3100. Pre-requisite: EESC2010 or ESSC2010 or permission of instructor.
description: This course is an important part of the core Earth and Environmental Sciences Curriculum. It introduces the processes and products of rock deformation in three dimensions, ranging from micro- (micron) to macro- (kilometer) scales. It discusses geometries and mechanism of faults, folds, structural features of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, and superposed deformations and introduces regional deformational history and tectonics. Structural geology in the field of resource exploration (petroleum and mineral deposits) is also introduced. Class lectures are supplemented by lab exercise and demonstrations as well as field trips to local or overseas outcrops.

Labs use geological maps, computers, stereonets, and physical analogs to illustrate these concepts. Students are encouraged to lead discussion of leading geological topics spread throughout the semester, each of which integrates recent class topics with large-scale active tectonics. Field trips in the second half of the semester encourage small-group discussion of observations and interpretations of deformational history of the field working area. The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. description: EESC3140 is designed to introduce students to the global distribution of elements and the chemistry of natural Earth's materials. The course focuses on understanding the chemical processes operating within the solid Earth and other planets, spanning from the past to the present. Emphasis is placed on developing quantitative and analytical skills in geochemistry. The course covers a wide range of topics, including fundamental principles of geochemical processes, thermal dynamics, phase transitions and the relationship between pressure, temperature, and composition in different geological materials, major elements, trace elements, rare Earth elements, element mobility and mineral stability, and the roles of different elements in Earth’s evolution. The course also introduces the role of minerals and rocks in supporting and influencing life and, how biological processes affect the chemical composition of Earth’s atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere. Students will be trained to acquire a comprehensive understanding of the formation and interaction of materials within the Earth. Students will learn about the geochemical processes involved and their implications for potential tectonic settings and surficial processes. By studying geochemical data and engaging in practical sessions, students will develop the skills to analyze and interpret the geochemical data, allowing them to discuss paleo-environments with possible tectonic models such as seafloor spreading, subduction and mountain building regimes.

description: This course explores the fundamental dynamical processes that govern atmospheric motion, with a focus on the physical mechanisms driving weather systems and large-scale circulation. Building on foundational fluid dynamics, students will develop a deeper understanding of the equations of motion and their applications to atmospheric phenomena.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to Recall and explain the fundamental equations and physical principles governing atmospheric motion.  Apply key dynamical models, such as the shallow water and quasi-geostrophic equations, to analyze atmospheric flows.  Analyze wave phenomena and instabilities, including Rossby waves, gravity waves, and baroclinic instability.  Evaluate the interactions between waves and mean flows, and assess their role in shaping atmospheric circulation.  Interpret and communicate insights from weather-in-a-tank experiments to illustrate complex atmospheric dynamics.

Shallow Water Equations – Derivation and applications in modeling large-scale atmospheric flows.  Quasi-Geostrophic Motion – Balance approximations and their role in midlatitude dynamics.  Rossby Waves – Planetary wave dynamics and their implications for weather patterns.  Gravity Waves – Generation and propagation.  Barotropic and Baroclinic Instability – Mechanisms of atmospheric instability and storm development.  Wave-Mean-Flow Interactions – Feedbacks between waves and background flow.  Vorticity Dynamics – Absolute, relative, and potential vorticity in atmospheric motion.  Tropical Circulation – Dynamics of the Hadley cell and its thermodynamic and hydrodynamic constraints.  Extratropical Circulation – Dynamics of Ferrel cell and jet streams.  Wave Diagnostics – Analyzing wave source, waveguide, and wave propagation.  Wave Activity and Blocking – Understanding persistent weather pattern dynamics using wave activity.

title: Global Environmental Change
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC3800.
description: This course includes the science behind the global warming issue, how the public views the issue and the critical thinking needed to analyze the evidence seen in the media/articles from the point of view of scientists. The world energy use, which is considered to be the cause of global warming, and the impacts are discussed in the course. In this course, students will learn about the radiation budgets/balance in the atmosphere, possible climate forcings that can upset the energy balance, how the earth’s global average temperature is measured, why global warming is described as “the biggest hoax” in human history, observations from the ocean and cryosphere and popular environmental issues/arguments discussed in the mainstream media. Newest observations from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report are included throughout the course.This course actively incorporates elements of innovation, design, global citizenship and social enterprisingness by asking the students to think innovatively but critically about possible solutions to adapt to and combat climate change and the global energy/health crisis. Different options including their pros and cons are actively discussed in class. Students are encouraged to think creatively about the problem from different angles, e.g., by standing in the shoes of climate skeptics – evaluating their “data”, how they present them, the arguments put forth by them – in order to develop a strategic approach to best communicate the issues to a variety of stakeholders. Project assignments will allow students to focus on one particular environmental issue in other part of the world, attempting to address the issue in the very different geographical, cultural, economic and political contexts from that of the students. Example projects can be “How to use geoengineering to combat climate change?”, “How can Sub-Saharan Africa secure its future food supply under the threat of climate change?”, etc. In the course, students will define and understand the problem. They shall form groups and discuss their own point of views and search information on the evidence of the corresponding arguments.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to gain understanding of basic climate science behind the global warming issue, including how Earth’s global temperature has been measured by scientists and how the global average temperature is calculated study observations from different components of Earth besides the atmosphere, such as ocean and cryosphere observations, and how these components are affected by the human activities study how the scientific problem is presented and perceived in the society and learn how to use one’s scientific knowledge to identify possible solutionsThe active incorporation of elements of innovation and design in the course is critical in allowing the students to develop a keen scientific mindset and logic flow to understand the complexity of the climate change and energy issues (Learning Outcome #1), and to dissect the reasons behind contradictory arguments in a society (Learning Outcome #3). Critical evaluation of the arguments from both sides (climate alarmists vs. skeptics) will ultimately allow them to develop their own stance in the issue, and think critically about the ways to move the world forward towards sustainability (Learning Outcome #3). The incorporation of global citizenship and social enterprisingness is also crucial for students to develop a keen awareness of how environmental issues affect people in a huge variety of geographical and cultural contexts (Learning Outcome #2), and think critically about what kinds of solutions best fit a certain region (Learning Outcome #3).

description: This course introduces the role of engineering geologists and the application of engineering geological principles to various civil engineering works. The course covers the key concepts and skills in site investigation, soil and rock description, engineering geological assessments and reporting. Topics include ground investigation, slope engineering, foundation engineering, tunneling and cavern development, and marine works. title: Applied Geophysics
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4110. Pre-requisite: (EESC2010 or ESSC2010) and (EESC3120 or ESSC3120).
description: This course introduces concepts, principles, and applications of geophysical methods in environmental and engineering studies. It offers an overall survey of various geophysical methods for exploring the shallow subsurface. It provides the technical foundation needed to understand the use and limitations of gravity, seismic, ground penetrating radar, and electromagnetic methods. Demonstration of commonly used methods will be provided in the field along with tutorials of preliminary data analysis techniques.

title: Advanced Geosciences Field Study I
components:

requirements: Not for students who have taken EESC3110 or ESSC3110. Pre-requisite: (EESC2010 or ESSC2010) and [(EESC3100 or ESSC3100) or (EESC4120 or ESSC4120)], or by instructor’s approval.
description: Understanding Earth processes and environmental changes over geological time requires the experience and skills gained from fieldwork. EESC4119 is an advanced-level course of the Earth and Environmental Sciences Programme. It covers important aspects of field geology, including petrology, structural geology, tectonics, geophysics, and surficial processes. The principal goal of this course is to train students to recognize different lithological units and their spatial relationship in three dimensions, and to understand the related tectonic environment and formation mechanisms. Class lectures introduce basic skills of reading and interpreting geological maps, using geological equipment (i.e., compass-clinometer, GPS receiver), and producing field notes and reports. Field projects include field observation and description, techniques for field data acquisition and analysis, sample collection, and geological map compilation. Field projects also focus on surficial processes, which occur over relatively short geological timescales but play important roles in environment and ecology. The field location, whether in mainland China or overseas, may change from year to year.

title: Petrology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4120. Pre-requisite: EESC2010 or ESSC2010.
description: Petrology is an essential subfield of Earth and Environmental Sciences because the rock record is the foundation for interpreting Earth history and internal processes. Petrologic concepts help us understand the Earth system, with connections to related fields such as geochemistry, geophysics, mineralogy, structural geology and geodynamics. This course broadly surveys the formation, distribution, chemical composition, mineral associations, and internal texture and structures in rocks of the earth’s crust and upper mantle, and establishes it relation to global tectonic environments. Class lectures are supplemented by lab exercise, demonstrations and tutorials (e.g. study of rock hand specimens, understand phase rule, use of optical microscope etc.).
outcome: Students are expected to gain the following abilities: Gain the skills to identify different rock types (igneous and metamorphic basically). Good knowledge of typical mineral assemblages of different rocks. Use optical polarizing microscope to distinguish: (1) different minerals based on their optical properties, (2) typical igneous and metamorphic micro-textures and structures, (3) featured mineral assemblages corresponding to different P-T conditions. Understand phase equilibrium and phase rule and their applications in understanding the rock forming process. Understand different metamorphic facies and their significance of variable tectonic settings. Use petrologic concepts and theories to address topics of societal interests, including natural hazards, natural resources, and human health issues. The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Advanced Geosciences Field Study II
requirements: Pre-requisite: (EESC2010 or ESSC2010) or (EESC2119 or EESC2129) or EESC2160 or (EESC3100 or ESSC3100) or EESC3140 or (EESC4120 or ESSC4120) or with course coordinator’s approval
description: EESC4129 is a comprehensive course designed to provide students with a deep understanding of plate tectonics, advanced geological field techniques, and their applications in engineering and water resources. The course aims to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of plate tectonics, including sea floor spreading, subduction, and mineral deposits. Additionally, it focuses on teaching students advanced geological field techniques and their practical application in field studies. The course also addresses engineering problems related to geological factors and explores the significance of water resources within a geological context. EESC4129 incorporates a combination of theoretical knowledge and practical training. The course includes 10 lectures covering essential concepts and techniques, plus 14 days in the field and engage in onsite discussions. Students will have the opportunity to visit a geologically significant area to gain firsthand experience and understanding of the geological setting, formation processes, tectonic history, and their relationship with urban planning. This field study will provide students with a solid background in local geology and geomorphology, enabling them to comprehend the geological processes and their implications in various settings. Students will engage in a mapping exercise, where they will collect geological data, perform detailed field observations, and analyze their findings. This exercise will enhance their critical thinking skills and equip them with the ability to plan geological projects effectively. Additionally, students will receive training in life-saving skills to ensure their safety during fieldwork. By the end of the course, students will have developed a heightened awareness of the interplay between geology and urban planning, contributing to their holistic understanding of the natural environment.

title: Geomorphology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4130. Pre-requisite: EESC3100 or ESSC3100.
description: This course is an important part of the core Earth and Environmental Sciences Curriculum. It introduces the main concepts in geomorphology with emphasis on understanding the coupling of environments, processes and materials that leads to landform development. Understanding the underlying geological principles of rocks, minerals, structural deformation and geological time are important background knowledge to be enhanced by the study of geomorphology.It discusses the qualitative and quantitative techniques for investigation and research in the field, laboratory, and computer simulation. The application of geomorphology for public safety, engineering problems and development of sustainable solutions will be emphasized. Examples from theory and practice of geomorphology in Hong Kong will be introduced. Practical understanding and skills will be gained from lab exercises and field trips in Hong Kong.Students are suggested to be equipped with basic knowledge of rocks and minerals, structural geology and geological time scale.

title: Seismology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4140. Pre-requisite: (EESC3120 or ESSC3120) or ESSC3010.
description: This course focuses on the concepts and theory of elastic wave propagation and physics of earthquake. The topics covered include the Earth’s internal structure, material elasticity, travel time tomography, seismic ray theory, ray tracing, and earthquake source parameter. Methods and field practice of seismological survey will also be introduced.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to know about Earth’s inner structure, understand principles of elastic wave propagation and earthquake physics, seismic imaging, as well as seismic exploration. The students will also be trained with extensive computing exercises. The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Volcanoes
description: On any given day, ~20 subaerial volcanoes worldwide are erupting. Even more submarine volcanoes are probably erupting without being detected. Volcanic eruptions can have devastating economic and social consequences, but are also the fundamental force that builds the majority of our planet’s surface. Volcanic eruptions and emissions can also affect atmospheric and climate conditions. This course will explore the various techniques used to study volcanoes’ underlying structure as well as their precursory and eruptive activity.

components:

requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4160. Pre-requisite: (EESC3120 or ESSC3120) or ESSC3010 or (EESC4010 or ESSC4010).
description: This course focuses on the concepts and theory of marine geology and geophysics. Marine geology is distinct from that of continent and is the important foundation to launch Plate Tectonics, the modern unified theory of the Earth. In this course, major components of marine geological settings such as mid-ocean ridges, transform faults, subduction zones, oceanic lithosphere, and etc. will be introduced and discussed in details. Methods of geophysical survey will also be introduced. Field experiments of scientific instruments such as Ocean Bottom Seismometers, marine magnetometer and gravimeter will be conducted. A geological field trip will also be included. This course will be jointly offered with Ocean College, Zhejiang University, as an initiative to develop ocean sciences at CUHK.

title: Geodynamics
requirements: Pre-requisite: EESC2010 or ESSC2010.
description: What is the mechanism of plate tectonics and a variety of geological phenomena, such as seafloor spreading, mountain building, volcanoes, earthquakes, faulting? Geodynamics is going to answer those questions through observations and models of the large-scale behaviors of the solid Earth. The goal of the course is to develop a thorough understanding of physical processes, such as lithospheric deformation, heat transfer, and mantle flow. Lectures, paper discussions, and tutorials will help you to understand the principle of geodynamics, learn how to develop simple but useful models, and explain how the Earth evolves.
outcome: Understand the fundamental geodynamics principles. Know how to find and process geophysical data, such as topography, gravity, and earthquakes. Able to build and solve geodynamic models and use the model results to explain a variety of geological phenomena. Acquire the ability to read and summarize literatures effectively and efficiently.  Develop critical thinking on the previous studies.

title: Earthquake Source Physics
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4180. Pre-requisite: (EESC3120 or ESSC3120) or (EESC4010 or ESSC4010) or (EESC4140 or ESSC4140).
description: This course focuses on the concepts and theory of earthquake source physics. The topics covered include seismic instrumentation, geophysical observations of earthquake source processes, kinematic source representation of earthquakes, dynamic rupture propagation of earthquakes, frictional properties of fault zones, and entire earthquake cycle. Methods and field practice of seismological survey will also be introduced.

title: Land-Atmosphere Interactions and Boundary-Layer Meteorology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4210. Pre-requisite: (EESC2020 or ESSC2020) or (EESC3200 or ESSC3200) or permission of instructor.
description: This course introduces the physical, chemical and biological processes governing the exchange of energy, momentum, water and other chemical materials between the atmosphere and land surface, including a formal introduction into boundary-layer meteorology. Topics covered include the basic equations and concepts of heat, momentum and mass conservation and transfer at the land-atmosphere interface; soil physics and hydrometeorology; temperature, humidity and wind distribution in the atmospheric boundary layer; theories and observations of turbulence; boundary layer dynamics; biometeorology and ecophysiology of land plants; canopy and ecosystem exchange; and land use change and urbanization. Applications to weather phenomena, air pollution, forestry, agriculture and ecosystem management will be emphasized throughout.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to 1) Gain knowledge of physical, chemical and biological processes of land-atmosphere interactions and boundary layer dynamics; and 2) Develop the skill and ability to understand weather and climate variability related to land-atmosphere interactions. (Course Outcomes as related to Programme Learning Outcomes) -- The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Tropical Meteorology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4220. Pre-requisite: EESC3200 or ESSC3200.
description: This course introduces tropical atmospheric circulation and related air-sea coupling at a variety of spatial and temporal scales. The topics covered include the role of the tropics in the global energy and momentum balance, ITCZ, subtropical high, upper-level anticyclones, tropical ocean circulation, tropical weather, climate and atmosphere-ocean interaction phenomena including meso-scale convective systems, tropical waves, the Hadley and the Walker circulation, El Nino-Southern Oscillation, tropical cyclones, Madden Julian Oscillation, and monsoons.

title: Introduction to the Physics and Chemistry of Aerosol
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4230. Pre-requisite: EESC2020 or ESSC2020 or permission of instructor.
description: Fundamentals of aerosol physics and chemistry; condensation and evaporation; thermodynamics; nucleation, diffusion, coagulation; radiative, hygroscopic properties, and cloud formation potential of aerosols; aerosol phase oxidation reactions; heterogeneous oxidative processes.

title: Air Pollution Science and Engineering
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4240.
description: This course will cover a variety of topics related to air pollution science and engineering. Topics include: indoor and outdoor air quality (including particulate matters (PM) and gases pollutants); air pollution measurement and statistics; air quality meteorology and dispersion models; principles and challenges of air pollution control and measurement.

To understand the working principles of various air pollution monitoring instrumentation.  To apply statistical tools and mathematical models to solve air pollutant dispersion problems.  To apply various air pollution engineering approaches to solve air pollution issues. title: General Circulation and Climate Models
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4250. Pre-requisite: EESC3200 or ESSC3200 or permission of instructor.

title: Urban Climatology
requirements: Not for students who have taken ESSC4260. Pre-requisite: EESC2020 or ESSC2020.
description: Human modifications to the surface of the Earth during urbanisation change most of the elements of climate and weather in the urban atmosphere. This course introduces the fundamentals of urban climatology and the processes caused by the changes in the surface environment, particularly focusing on how urban structures interact with the atmospheric environment. Numerical modelling and field techniques are introduced to understand the underlying processes resulting urban climatic phenomena. It also examines the implications on human comfort and climate-sensitive urban planning and design, as well as the relationship between cities and climate change

title: Cloud Dynamics
requirements: Pre-requisite: EESC2020 or ESSC2020.
description: This course presents an introduction to the science of clouds. We begin with a descriptive cloud classification to introduce the different types of clouds in the Earth’s atmosphere. The roles of aerosols in cloud are also discussed. This is followed by cloud microphysics, describing the basic microphysical processes regarding formation, growth, shrinkage, breakup and fallout of cloud and precipitation particles. Next, different structures of precipitation and radar cloud sensing are presented. This will then be linked to cloud dynamics, associated with the fluid motions of the atmosphere. Student taking this course are expected to have taken EESC2020 or ESSC2020.

title: Practical Meteorology
requirements: Pre-requisite: EESC2020 or ESSC2020.
description: Practical Meteorology is an advanced undergraduate course designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of various aspects of meteorology and their practical applications. The course will cover synoptic and mesoscale meteorology, satellite and radar meteorology, radiative transfer, lidar meteorology, aviation meteorology, and atmospheric instrumentation. Through a combination of lectures and case studies using instrument data, students will gain hands-on experience in analyzing and interpreting meteorological data.

title: Chemistry of Aquatic and Terrestrial Organic Matter

Students will learn about the sources, transformation, and fate of organic matter in natural systems, as well as the impact of human activities on organic matter cycling. Topics may include the structure and function of organic molecules, biogeochemical processes involving organic matter, analytical techniques for studying organic matter, and the role of organic matter in ecosystem functioning. This course may also explore the implications of organic matter chemistry for environmental quality, carbon cycling, and nutrient dynamics in natural systems. Advisory: 2 years college course works in Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics is recommended.

Describe the sources, transformation, and fate of organic matter in natural systems. Analyse the impact of human activities on organic matter cycling in ecosystems. Apply analytical techniques to study organic matter in environmental samples. Evaluate the role of organic matter in ecosystem functioning and environmental quality. Discuss the implications of organic matter chemistry for carbon cycling and nutrient dynamics in natural systems.

title: Advanced Environmental Chemistry
requirements: Not for students who have taken ENSC4525. Pre-requisite: EESC2515 or ENSC2515 or permission of the instructor.
description: This course is designed to extend students' understanding of and develop their ability in the application of various aspects of environmental chemistry in relation to the major types of air and water pollution associated with industrial and vehicle emissions. It outlines the basic processes in bleaching and dyeing, electroplating and food processing that give rise to water pollution and application of physico-chemical techniques in controlling such pollution. It also examines combustion processes and the associated applications and limitations of the absorption, adsorption, oxidation-reduction and catalytic conversion techniques in relation to aerial emissions from furnaces and vehicles. Site visits will be arranged where possible to enhance students' ability in application.

title: Biogeochemistry
requirements:

description: This course presents the recent understanding and advancements in global biogeochemistry. The lectures are on a range of topics, covering major elemental cycles from the early Earth to future projections and from the lithosphere to the atmosphere, with an emphasis on the Ocean. Advanced concepts of application of biogeochemistry will further be discussed with an emphasis on environmental pollution and global climate change. The fundamentals of major elemental cycles like carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, oxygen, sulphur, and silicate will also be covered.

Apply biogeochemistry concepts to global issues like pollution and climate change.  Evaluate research on major elemental cycles, including carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, oxygen, sulfur, and silicate.

title: Practical Atmospheric Modeling
requirements: Pre-requisite: (EESC2020 or ESSC2020) and (MATH2550 or EESC2520 or PHYS2051) and (PHYS1001 or 1002 or 1111 or 1113), or permission of instructor.
description: This course introduces the basic approach in working with LINUX and fundamental principles of atmospheric modeling and provides hands-on practice to perform numerical simulations on University computing cluster. It begins with the concept of model and reviewing of physical and chemical processes in the atmosphere. After that, this course will cover introduction and hands-on practice of the three basic processes in atmospheric simulation: pre-processing data, modeling, and post-processing data. The pre-processing process refers to the preparation of data from various sources by different techniques such as the generation of emission inventories for atmospheric chemistry modeling. It then introduces numerical modeling basics such as “model equations and numerical approaches”. For post-processing, this course offers different skills in visualization of the model output and evaluation of model output against real-world observations. This course also introduces advanced knowledge in “model coupling” and “inverse modeling”. Finally, this course provides hands-on practice on simple model development experiments. During the course, we will cover basic Linux environment commands to perform the main tasks mentioned above. Overall, students can anticipate grasping basic modeling concepts and skills from this course, which are of great value to their future careers in both academia and industry.
outcome: Able to explain the major chemical and physical processes that affect the spatiotemporal variations of major atmospheric composition. Explain the basic framework of atmospheric chemistry models including their input and output. Capable of visualizing model outputs and evaluating model outputs against observations. Have the skills to sort out model structure by reading model codes and then revise model codes according to research needs.

title: Research Frontiers in Earth & Environmental Sciences II
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5002.
description: Continuation of EESC5001. Recent research methods, experimental and computational techniques applied in Earth & Environmental Sciences. Topics extend over a diversity of research areas in Earth & Environmental Sciences, with a consistent theme that many of the operative processes are intertwined and advances in elucidating them hinge on the adoption of an interdisciplinary framework.

title: Solid and Fluid Mechanics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion(s): ESSC3010, ESSC4010, EESC4010, EASC5010.
description: This course presents the fundamentals of continuum mechanics illustrated with earth system science applications. Background materials on matrices, vectors and differential operators are first reviewed. The following topics will be covered: tensors and their properties; stress and strain; constitutive equations for Hookean elastic solid and Newtonian viscous fluid; mechanical properties and rheology of geomaterials; Eulerian and Lagrangian kinematics; momentum equations; vorticity and divergence; applications in geomechanics, seismology, atmospheric dynamics, and oceanography.

title: Soil Mechanics and Its Applications
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5020.
description: A survey of basic concepts of soil mechanics: Classification and physical properties of soil; stress and strain; pore pressure, seepage theory and effective stress; elastic solutions; shear strength and Mohr-Coulomb theory; failure mode and criteria; soil consolidation; lateral earth pressure; slope stability; bearing capacity and foundation designs; pile analyses and designs; soil improvement and soil nailing. Geotechnical applications: shallow and deep foundations; retaining structures; slope instability.
outcome: An understanding of the basics of poromechanics: stress and strain, pore pressure and effective stress, shear strength and failure criteria. Knowledge of the classification and physical properties of soil. A basic understanding of the mechanics of soil, soil consolidation and shear failure. An appreciation of the application of soil mechanics to geotechnical designs and engineering.
syllabus: A survey of basic concepts of soil mechanics: Classification and physical properties of soil.  Physical properties of soil. Seepage and effective stress, Pore pressure. Stress and strain. Shear strength. Soil consolidation. Geotechnical applications: shallow and deep foundations; retaining structures; slope instability. Laboratory measurement of soil deformation and strength.

title: Advanced Topics in Geophysics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5101.
description: Recent advances in theoretical and applied geophysics, with focus on geodesy, seismology, geoelectricity, geomagnetism and gravity, and their applications in natural hazard reduction, energy resources and environmental issues.

title: Aerosol Physics and Chemistry
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5103.
description: Knowledge of aerosol physics and chemistry such as condensation and evaporation; thermodynamics; radiative, hygroscopic properties, and cloud formation potential of aerosols;Recent advances in aerosol physics and chemistry researches; Roles of atmospheric aerosols on the critical environmental issues such as air quality, tropospheric smog, and climate change, with focus on observations, laboratory measurements and modelling.

title: General Circulation and Climate Models
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5104.
description: This course is about the general circulations of the atmosphere, ocean, the interactions among them and with other components of the Earth System, as well as their simulations using climate models, in the context of climate variability and climate change. Topics include basic fluid dynamics of large-scale atmosphere and ocean circulations, radiative transfer, atmospheric general circulation, mid latitude dynamics, ocean general circulation, general circulation models, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to1) Gain fundamental concepts of the general circulations of the atmosphere and oceans;2) Understand how they are simulated in climate models;3) Develop the ability to analyze and explain climate phenomena, including human-related climate change, based on climate modelling results. (Course outcomes as related to Programme Learning Outcomes) -- The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Applied Geophysics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5110.
description: This course introduces concepts, principles, and applications of geophysical methods in environmental and engineering studies. It offers an overall survey of various geophysical methods for exploring the shallow subsurface. It provides the technical foundation needed to understand the use and limitations of gravity, seismic, ground penetrating radar, and electromagnetic methods. Demonstration of commonly used methods will be provided in the field along with tutorials of preliminary data analysis techniques. Technical papers published in leading applied geophysics journals will be discussed in reading groups.

title: Petrology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5120.
description: Petrology is an essential subfield of Earth System Science because the rock record is the foundation for interpreting Earth history and internal processes. Petrologic concepts help us understand the Earth system, with connections to related fields such as geochemistry, geophysics, mineralogy, structural geology and geodynamics. This course broadly surveys the formation, distribution, chemical composition, mineral associations, and internal texture and structures in rocks of the earth’s crust and upper mantle, and establishes it relation to global tectonic environments. Class lectures are supplemented by lab exercise, demonstrations and tutorials (e.g. study of rock hand specimens, understand phase rule, use of optical microscope etc.).
outcome: Students are expected to gain the following abilities: Gain the skills to identify different rock types (igneous and metamorphic basically). Good knowledge of typical mineral assemblages of different rocks. Use optical polarizing microscope to distinguish: (1) different minerals based on their optical properties, (2) typical igneous and metamorphic micro-textures and structures, (3) featured mineral assemblages corresponding to different P-T conditions.  Understand phase equilibrium and phase rule and their applications in understanding the rock forming process. Understand different metamorphic facies and their significance of variable tectonic settings. Use petrologic concepts and theories to address topics of societal interests, including natural hazards, natural resources, and human health issues. The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Geomorphology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences or grant the approval from course coordinator;Pre-requisite(s): ESSC/EESC2010 and ESSC/EESC3100 or permission of instructor;Exclusion: EASC5130.
description: This course is an important part of the core Earth and Environmental Sciences Curriculum. It introduces the main concepts in geomorphology with emphasis on understanding the coupling of environments, processes and materials that leads to landform development. Understanding the underlying geological principles of rocks, minerals, structural deformation and geological time are important background knowledge to be enhanced by the study of geomorphology.It discusses the qualitative and quantitative techniques for investigation and research in the field, laboratory, and computer modeling. The application of geomorphology for public safety, engineering problems and development of sustainable solutions will be emphasized. Examples from theory and practice of geomorphology in Hong Kong will be introduced. Practical understanding and skills will be gained from lab exercises and field trips in Hong Kong.Students are suggested to be equipped with basic knowledge of rocks and minerals, structural geology and geological time scale.

title: Seismology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5140.
description: This course focuses on the concepts and theory of elastic wave propagation and physics of earthquake. The topics covered include the Earth’s internal structure, material elasticity, travel time tomography, seismic ray theory, ray tracing, and earthquake source parameter. Methods and field practice of seismological survey and programming methods of data processing will also be introduced.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to know about Earth’s inner structure, understand principles of elastic wave propagation and earthquake physics, seismic imaging, as well as seismic exploration. The students will also be trained with extensive computing exercises. The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Volcanoes
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5150.
description: On any given day, ~20 subaerial volcanoes worldwide are erupting. Even more submarine volcanoes are probably erupting without being detected. Volcanic eruptions can have devastating economic and social consequences, but are also the fundamental force that builds the majority of our planet’s surface. Volcanic eruptions and emissions can also affect atmospheric and climate conditions. This course will explore the various techniques used to study volcanoes’ underlying structure as well as their precursory and eruptive activity.

title: Geodynamics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5170.
description: What is the mechanism of plate tectonics and a variety of geological phenomena, such as seafloor spreading, mountain building, volcanoes, earthquakes, faulting? Geodynamics is going to answer those questions through observations and models of the large-scale behaviors of the solid Earth. The goal of the course is to develop a thorough understanding of physical processes, such as lithospheric deformation, heat transfer, and mantle flow. Lectures, paper discussions, and tutorials will help you to understand the principle of geodynamics, learn how to develop simple but useful models, and explain how the Earth evolves.
outcome: Understand the fundamental geodynamics principles. Know how to find and process geophysical data, such as topography, gravity, and earthquakes. Able to build and solve geodynamic models and use the model results to explain a variety of geological phenomena. Acquire the ability to read and summarize literatures effectively and efficiently. Develop critical thinking on the previous studies.

title: Earthquake Source Physics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5180.
description: This course focuses on the concepts and theory of earthquake source physics. The topics covered include seismic instrumentation, geophysical observations of earthquake source processes, kinematic source representation of earthquakes, dynamic rupture propagation of earthquakes, frictional properties of fault zones, and entire earthquake cycle. Methods and field practice of seismological survey will also be introduced.

title: Land-Atmosphere Interactions and Boundary-Layer Meteorology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5210.
description: This course introduces the physical, chemical and biological processes governing the exchange of energy, momentum, water and other chemical materials between the atmosphere and land surface, including a formal introduction into boundary-layer meteorology. Topics covered include the basic equations and concepts of heat, momentum and mass conservation and transfer at the land-atmosphere interface; soil physics and hydrometeorology; temperature, humidity and wind distribution in the atmospheric boundary layer; theories and observations of turbulence; stability and boundary-layer dynamics; biometeorology and ecophysiology of land plants; canopy and ecosystem exchange; and land use change and urbanization. Applications to weather phenomena, air pollution, forestry, agriculture and ecosystem management will be emphasized throughout.
outcome: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to 1) Gain knowledge of physical, chemical and biological processes of land-atmosphere interactions and boundary layer dynamics; and 2) Develop the skill and ability to understand weather and climate variability related to land-atmosphere interactions. (Course Outcomes as related to Programme Learning Outcomes) -- The students will develop: 1) the ability to evaluate an issue critically based on evidence and scientific principle, 2) to acquire knowledge effectively by self-study and using information technology, and to work independently, 3) to work effectively in a team, and 4) to present information in a clear, concise and logical manner. The students also can acquire a responsible attitude in study and work, and have motivation for life-long learning.

title: Tropical Meteorology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5220.
description: This course introduces tropical atmospheric circulation and related air-sea coupling at a variety of spatial and temporal scales. The topics covered include the role of the tropics in the global energy and momentum balance, ITCZ, subtropical high, upper-level anticyclones, tropical ocean circulation, tropical weather, climate and atmosphere-ocean interaction phenomena including meso-scale convective systems, tropical waves, the Hadley and the Walker circulation, El Nino-Southern Oscillation, tropical cyclones, Madden Julian Oscillation, and monsoons.

title: Air Pollution Science and Engineering
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5240.
description: This course will cover a variety of topics related to air pollution science and engineering. Topics include: indoor and outdoor air quality (including particulate matters (PM) and gases pollutants); air pollution measurement and statistics; air quality meteorology and dispersion models; principles and challenges of air pollution control and measurement.
outcome: To understand the physical and chemical principles governing the sources, formation, transport, transformation, health impacts of air pollutants in both indoor and outdoor environments. To understand the working principles of various air pollution monitoring instrumentation.  To apply statistical tools and mathematical models to solve air pollutant dispersion problems.  To apply various air pollution engineering approaches to solve air pollution issues. To gain a better understanding of current air pollution problems and control challenges.

title: Urban Climatology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5260
description: Human modifications to the surface of the Earth during urbanisation change most of the elements of climate and weather in the urban atmosphere. This course introduces the fundamentals of urban climatology and the processes caused by the changes in the surface environment, particularly focusing on how urban structures interact with the atmospheric environment. Numerical modelling and field techniques are introduced to understand the underlying processes resulting urban climatic phenomena. It also examines the implications on human comfort and climate-sensitive urban planning and design, as well as the relationship between cities and climate change.

title: Cloud Dynamics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5270.
description: This course presents an introduction to the science of clouds. We begin with a descriptive cloud classification to introduce the different types of clouds in the Earth’s atmosphere. The roles of aerosols in cloud are also discussed. This is followed by cloud microphysics, describing the basic microphysical processes regarding formation, growth, shrinkage, breakup and fallout of cloud and precipitation particles. Next, different structures of precipitation and radar cloud sensing are presented. This will then be linked to cloud dynamics, associated with the fluid motions of the atmosphere.

title: Practical Meteorology
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EASC5280.
description: Practical Meteorology is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of various aspects of meteorology and their practical applications. The course will cover synoptic and mesoscale meteorology, satellite and radar meteorology, radiative transfer, lidar meteorology, aviation meteorology, and atmospheric instrumentation. Through a combination of lectures and case studies using instrument data, students will gain hands-on experience in analyzing and interpreting meteorological data.

title: Biogeochemistry of Aquatic and Terrestrial Organic Matter

description: The course "Biogeochemistry of Aquatic and Terrestrial Organic Matter" covers the study of the chemical composition, properties, and reactivity of organic matter in aquatic and terrestrial environments. Students will learn about the sources, transformation, and fate of organic matter in natural systems, as well as the impact of human activities on organic matter cycling. Topics may include the structure and function of organic molecules, biogeochemical processes involving organic matter, analytical techniques for studying organic matter, and the role of organic matter in ecosystem functioning. This course may also explore the implications of organic matter biogeochemistry for environmental quality, carbon cycling, and nutrient dynamics in natural systems. Advisory: 2 years college course works in Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics is recommended.

Describe the sources, transformation, and fate of organic matter in natural systems. Analyse the impact of human activities on organic matter cycling in ecosystems. Apply analytical techniques to study organic matter in environmental samples. Evaluate the role of organic matter in ecosystem functioning and environmental quality. Discuss the implications of organic matter chemistry for carbon cycling and nutrient dynamics in natural systems.

description: This course presents the recent understanding and advancements in global biogeochemistry. The lectures are on a range of topics, covering major elemental cycles from the early Earth to future projections and from the lithosphere to the atmosphere, with an emphasis on the Ocean. Advanced concepts of application of biogeochemistry will further be discussed with an emphasis on environmental pollution and global climate change. The fundamentals of major elemental cycles like carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, oxygen, sulphur, and silicate will also be covered.

Apply biogeochemistry concepts to global issues like pollution and climate change.  Critically evaluate research on major elemental cycles, including carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, oxygen, sulfur, and silicate.

title: Environmental Health: A Systems Thinking Approach
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences;Exclusion: EESC4350, LSCI5750
description: This graduate-level course explores the interdisciplinary field of environmental health through the lens of systems thinking. Students will examine how ecological, social, and technological systems interact to influence public health. Emphasis is placed on understanding complex interconnections and developing holistic solutions to environmental health challenges.
outcome: Apply systems thinking to analyze environmental health issues. Design and evaluate interventions that address complex health challenges. Communicate effectively with diverse stakeholders. Develop strategic plans for sustainable health improvements.

This course is a communication intensive course where students participate in their learning through various activities as Town Hall discussion, flipped classroom, group activities/discussion and student-as-partner lectures.

title: Statistical Methods and Data Analysis for Earth and Environmental Sciences
requirements:
For students in MPhil-PhD Earth and Environmental Sciences or MSc Earth and Environmental Analytics for Sustainability
Exclusion: EASC5510
description: This course covers the theoretical basis and practical applications of data analysis relevant for earth system science. This course aims to introduce students to Earth and environmental data manipulation, from sampling, reading and writing, to statistical analysis and parameter estimation, to time series analysis, to plotting and visualization. Topics include: digital signal processing, sampling techniques; probability distributions; hypothesis testing; correlation analysis; linear and nonlinear regression; statistical forecasting, harmonic analysis and spectral analysis; principle component analysis; and geostatistics. Tutorials will be based on real geophysical examples including remote sensing and in situ observations, as well as model data. Previous elementary coding experience in Python 3 is recommended.
outcome: Students will become knowledgeable about the acquisition, pre-processing and analysis of geophysical and environmental data, including remote sensing, in situ observation and model data. Students will acquire knowledge on techniques for data processing, including visualization methods and statistical analysis, and on the applications of these data and tools to geophysical and environmental problems. title: Practical Atmospheric Modeling

description: This course introduces the basic approach in working with LINUX and fundamental principles of atmospheric modeling and provides hands-on practice to perform numerical simulations on University computing cluster. It begins with the concept of model and reviewing of physical and chemical processes in the atmosphere. After that, this course will cover introduction and hands-on practice of the three basic processes in atmospheric simulation: pre-processing data, modeling, and post-processing data. The pre-processing process refers to the preparation of data from various sources by different techniques such as the generation of emission inventories for atmospheric chemistry modeling. It then introduces numerical modeling basics such as “model equations and numerical approaches”. For post-processing, this course offers different skills in visualization of the model output and evaluation of model output against real-world observations. This course also introduces advanced knowledge in “model coupling” and “inverse modeling”. Finally, this course provides hands-on practice on simple model development experiments. During the course, we will cover basic Linux environment commands to perform the main tasks mentioned above. Overall, students can anticipate grasping basic modeling concepts and skills from this course, which are of great value to their future careers in both academia and industry.

Capable of visualizing model outputs and evaluating model outputs against observations. Have the skills to sort out model structure by reading model codes and then revise model codes according to research needs.

outcome: Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:1.    Understand the science behind climate change and its financial impacts2.    Learn global climate regulations and their effects on financial institutions3.    Identify and model climate-related risks, including asset vulnerability and exposure4.    Quantify the financial impacts of climate-related risks on portfolios and businesses5.    Explore opportunities in sustainable investments and renewable energy6.    Understand climate adaptation plans and how they incorporate 'Net Zero' goals and financial strategies7.    Gain insights into green finance and the growth of sustainable markets

Emphasize the importance and impact of sustainable financial practices in supporting climate mitigation and adaptationClimate Risk Across Asset Classes-    Apply climate risk analysis to specific asset classes, including equity, debt, private equity, and real estate, and learn techniques for portfolio decarbonization and measuring financed GHG emissions
